idea: A river meander simulated in code (curvature-driven bank migration): a looping channel drawn year by year as nested lines, with the abandoned loops left behind as oxbow lakes. Caption: 'Rivers don't flow. They negotiate.' For anyone who loves a system that keeps rewriting its own map.

A drainage basin grown in code from a tilted noise landscape: thousands of thin tributaries merging into one trunk, drawn like a leaf's veins. Caption: 'Every river is a tree growing downhill.' A true geometry joke that rewards a second look.

The Mississippi's delta lobes drawn as overlapping fan outlines, one per shift of the river's course over roughly the last 7,000 years. Caption: 'The river keeps trying to leave. Held in place since 1963.' (the year the Old River Control Structure began operating, stopping the Atchafalaya capture).
A snow crystal grown by a Reiter-style cellular automaton: a six-fold lacy flake, white on black. Caption: 'Weather, one crystal at a time.' Pretty at a distance, mathematical up close.

The Beaufort scale as a stack of thirteen sea-surface profiles, force 0 to force 12, generated from summed sine waves growing in height down the shirt, each labelled with its number only. Caption: 'Beaufort, 1805.' (Francis Beaufort devised the scale in 1805.) A quiet nautical chart for people who read the shipping forecast.

Luke Howard's cloud classes drawn by code with noise-built line textures: cirrus, cumulus, stratus, nimbus in a row. Caption: 'Luke Howard, 1802, gave clouds names.' A reminder that a pharmacist's hobby gave the sky its vocabulary.

A nested field of curl-noise vortices, large whorls containing smaller whorls containing smaller ones. Caption: 'Big whorls have little whorls, which feed on their velocity, and little whorls have lesser whorls, and so on to viscosity.' (Lewis Fry Richardson, 1922, a riff on Swift.) For the physicist who also likes verse.

Richardson's 'forecast factory': a globe cut into a grid of cells drawn in code, ringed by a spherical hall. Caption: '64,000 computers. All human.' (In 1922 Richardson imagined 64,000 people calculating the world's weather in a hall.) The first numerical weather forecast, as a joke about staffing.

A fractal coastline drawn three times with three ruler lengths, each longer and smoother than the last. Caption: 'Spain says its border with Portugal is 987 km. Portugal says 1,214.' (Richardson's coastline paradox.) Wry, true, and about measurement.

A lightning bolt grown by a dielectric-breakdown simulation, with its dead-end branches left visible beside the one that connected. Caption: 'It tried every way down. You only saw the one that worked.' A point of view about luck and survivorship.

Raindrops drawn from the physics of their shape at increasing sizes: tiny ones perfect spheres, larger ones flattened like hamburger buns, the biggest ones bag-shaped just before they break. Caption: 'Raindrops are not teardrops.' A small myth corrected, and everyone has drawn it wrong.

A single closed streamline looping from river to sea to cloud and back to a river, drawn as a Lissajous-like line. Caption: 'All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full.' (Ecclesiastes 1:7.) The water cycle, 2,000+ years before anyone drew it as a diagram.

A day of tide drawn as the sum of its harmonic constituents: five thin sine waves (M2, S2, N2, K1, O1) stacked above the one jagged curve they add up to. Caption: 'The tide is a sum of waves.' A nod to Kelvin's tide-predicting machines; for anyone who likes to see the parts.

A Kármán vortex street simulated in code behind a single small island, alternating spirals trailing off downwind. Caption: 'Even an island leaves a wake in the clouds.' (Such vortex streets form downwind of the Juan Fernández Islands, seen from orbit.) A big idea on a very small dot.

A long-memory time series drawn as an annual river-level record that wanders in long runs of high and low years. Caption: 'Hurst, Nile, 1951: floods remember.' (H. E. Hurst's work on Nile records found persistent long-term patterns.) For those who suspect that bad years cluster.

An ensemble forecast: thirty trajectories that begin from almost the same point and fan apart into different weather. Caption: 'Same morning. Thirty different Thursdays.' An honest picture of why forecasts say 'chance of'.

Thiessen polygons drawn from a scatter of rain gauges, each cell shaded only by line density. Caption: 'Thiessen, 1911: every raindrop belongs to its nearest gauge.' (A method Alfred Thiessen proposed for averaging rainfall.) Cartographic and a little absurd.

The wake of a ship drawn by code: a V of crests with the Kelvin angle marked. Caption: '19.47 degrees. Every ship, every speed.' (Kelvin's wake half-angle, independent of speed in deep water.) A fact about the sea that surprises almost everyone.

A ray-traced raindrop with light entering, bouncing once and leaving at 42 degrees, then a second ring where it bounces twice and leaves at about 51. Caption: '42 degrees.' (Descartes computed the primary rainbow angle in 1637.) Minimal for people who get the reference.

A braided river generated in code: dozens of shallow channels weaving round gravel bars across a wide plain. Caption: 'Too much gravel for one channel.' (Braiding happens where a river carries more sediment than a single channel can move.) A point of view about what happens when there is too much to carry.
